title: State v. Nikhat
subcite: SC No. 908/2023 | FIR No. 290/2022, PS Seelampur | Court of the Addl. Sessions Judge-05 (Electricity), East, Karkardooma Courts, Delhi
court: Court of the Additional Sessions Judge-05 (Electricity), East District, Karkardooma Courts, Delhi
judge: Sh. Ashish Rastogi, Addl. Sessions Judge-05 (Electricity)
parties: State (BSES Yamuna Power Ltd.) v. Nikhat, R/o Seelampur, Delhi (registered consumer/owner of the inspected premises)
result: Convicted under Section 135 read with Section 150 (abetment), Electricity Act, 2003. Civil liability on the theft bill (Rs. 53,982/-) settled and the amount deposited during trial and an NOC issued. Matter posted for hearing on quantum of sentence.
statutes: Sections 135, 150 & 2(15) (and third proviso to s. 135(1)), Electricity Act, 2003

interpretations.interpretation: The Court treated clause (a) — tapping or making a connection with a licensee’s overhead, underground or service lines/wires — as the operative limb, the case being one of direct hooking rather than meter tampering (clauses (b)–(e) having no factual foundation). As the Act does not define “dishonestly,” the Court imported Section 24 IPC and treated through a wire tapped from the licensee’s distribution box, the premises having no meter as satisfying the requirement of dishonest intention.

interpretations.provision: Third Proviso to Section 135(1) — Presumption of Dishonest Use
interpretations.interpretation: Read as a reverse-onus clause: proof of an artificial or unauthorised means of abstraction raises a presumption of dishonest use “until the contrary is proved.” Reading it with the “shall presume” jurisprudence (Neeraj Dutt) and the rebuttal standard (Hiten P. Dalal), the Court held that the burden shifted to the accused to make innocence reasonably probable — a bare denial, without evidence of a lawful source or paid bills, could not discharge it.

'Consumer' under Section 2(15) includes the owner/registered consumer, not only the actual user; the owner is answerable for illegal abstraction found at the premises even where a tenant is the user (Lokesh Chandela).

A registered consumer/owner who consciously permits a tenant to draw an unauthorised supply abets the theft and is punishable u/s 150 with the principal's punishment; the abettor can be convicted even where the actual user has absconded or died and is never tried.

citations.case: Punjab State Electricity Board v. Ashwani Kumar
citations.principle: An inspection report prepared by Board officers in discharge of official duty carries a presumption of regularity; the onus lies on the consumer to rebut it by cogent evidence.

citations.case: Sushil Sharma v. BSES Rajdhani Power Ltd.
citations.principle: Non-examination of an independent/public witness is no infirmity where the inspecting officials are trustworthy and bear no enmity towards the accused.

citations.case: Lokesh Chandela v. State of NCT & Ors.
citations.principle: Both the user of electricity and the owner/registered consumer of the premises fall within “consumer” under Section 2(15), making the owner answerable for illegal abstraction found at the premises.
“Shall presume” denotes a compulsory legal presumption which the Court is bound to draw until the fact is disproved.

citations.case: Hiten P. Dalal v. Bratindranath Banerjee
citations.principle: A statutory presumption need not be conclusively disproved; the accused must adduce evidence making the defence reasonably probable to a prudent man.

citations.case: Mukesh Rastogi v. North Delhi Power Ltd.
citations.principle: The easiest rebuttal of the theft presumption is to produce paid electricity bills; under Section 106 of the Evidence Act the onus of proving lawful, metered use lies on the consumer.

significance.point: An owner can be convicted of abetment even where the user has absconded
significance.explanation: The registered consumer/owner who consciously permits an (unarrested, untried) tenant to draw an unauthorised supply is guilty under Section 135 r/w Section 150; the principal’s absence from the dock does not absolve the abettor.
The owner cannot disown liability for illegal abstraction at the premises merely because a tenant was the user (Lokesh Chandela).

significance.point: The reverse-onus presumption binds the owner-abettor
significance.explanation: Once the unauthorised means is proved, the owner must show lawful, metered use — paid bills under the Section 106 onus (Mukesh Rastogi) — failing which the compulsory presumption convicts.

significance.point: Settlement, deposit and even an NOC are not immunity
significance.explanation: Closing the civil account — paying the settled bill and taking an NOC — does not answer the Section 135 charge; the settlement is read as conduct corroborating the theft.

significance.point: Failure to seize the wire, amid resistance, is not fatal
significance.explanation: That the illegal wire could not be removed because of resistance at the spot did not weaken the prosecution — the tap was independently established by the videography and the officials’ consistent testimony.

significance.point: A public witness is not essential
significance.explanation: Official inspection testimony suffices absent shown enmity (Ashwani Kumar; Sushil Sharma).
